newsitem.title: POLAND: Fears grow for Polish state TV's independence.
newsitem.headline: Fears grow for Polish state TV's independence.

text.p: Poland's news media and opposition parties accused the ruling leftist coalition on Friday of tightening its grip over state television, the country's main news provider, before next month's general elections.

The outcry followed Thursday's decision by broadcast media authorities to appoint people linked to the parties in power, the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and the Peasant Party (PSL), to the television's new supervisory board.
"A black day for state television," "They take it all," read headlines in Friday newspapers.

The new nine-member board cleared by the National Radio and Television Council (KRRiT), the broadcast media watchdog, will include seven people connected with the coalition, who will be able to push through any programme and financial decision.
By law, the board members, which elect the television's management, are appointed for three years and cannot be removed for reasons other than bad health or crime.
KRRiT members linked to the ex-communists and peasants also pushed allies onto the supervisory board of state radio.

"This is a bid to grab as much power as possible before the elections. The ruling parties want to retain some powers after the polls, in case they lose," said Jan Palkowski, spokesman for the opposition Movement for the Reconstruction of Poland.

"This is an attack not only on media independence but also on democracy," commented Tomasz Tywonek, spokesman of the Solidarity Election Action (AWS) alliance, the main rival of the co-ruling ex-communists in the September 21 polls.
Andrzej Potocki of the centrist Union for Freedom party said state television's flagship evening news programme was like a branch of the government information office.
"We remember this kind of situation well from before 1989 (when communism fell)", spokesman Potocki told Reuters.
The only two people connected to the opposition that were appointed to the new television board on Thursday instantly quit in protest when they learned of the body's line-up.
"I was a candidate for the board of state television, not parties' television," said film director Wojciech Marczewski.

KRRiT members linked to the coalition defended the qualifications of the new board. "It is good that experts have been chosen, not politicians from the first echelons," Witold Grabos, an ex-communist Council member, told PAP news agency.
State television, with two nationwide and 11 regional channels, is the most powerful news medium despite growing competition from private stations that sprouted after 1989.

The extent of independence of Poland's state television has already been questioned by the European Union and the United States, after Peasant Party-linked Ryszard Miazek was made its president last year.

Concern was voiced earlier this year by a group of journalists and other employees who published a letter protesting against alleged attempts to politicise television and the chaos stemming from frequent management changes.

The controversial appointments to the television board prompted demands to amend the law on the KRRiT, so as the make it immune to political pressure from parliamentary parties and the president who currently elect the body.
"KRRiT has ceased to be independent. What has happened requires a public debate," said Andrzej Zarebski, one of four of the nine members of the Council linked with the opposition.
The Council was created in the early 1990s to safeguard broadcasters' independence and regulate the market.
